paper.title: Predicting and Repairing Merge Collapse in Large Language Models
paper.abstract: Abstract Large language models fine-tuned from a shared base can be merged by averaging their task vectors, but some merges collapse far below the base model, and common merge operators give no warning before evaluation. We show that one statistic of the specialists’ task vectors both predicts this collapse and calibrates its repair. The power that averaging removes equals the variance of the task vectors across specialists, our measure of interference. Under a working noise model, the disturbance that a merge injects grows with the merge coefficient and with interference, yielding a pre-merge score. In our experiments on twenty-two merge configurations from four model families, only destructive merges exceed a threshold on this score. We find that statistics of sign conflict between specialists, a common target of existing merge operators, are anti-predictive. We then predicted the outcomes of fourteen merges before evaluating them, and twelve predictions were correct, including the destructive outcome of a specialist pair pushed past the threshold by continued pretraining. To address this collapse, we introduce Prism , an operator that averages the task vectors first and then soft-thresholds each layer at a level set by the layer’s interference. Without data or tuning, Prism keeps all five destructive merges above the threshold within evaluation noise of the base model, where plain averaging falls at least 14.4 points below it or collapses entirely. We apply Prism only above the threshold and keep the plain average for merges below it, which include all fifteen harmless ones. Code is available at https://github.com/js-lee-AI/PRISM .

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Model merging combines several models fine-tuned from the same pretrained checkpoint into one model by operating directly on their weights, with no further training ( Wortsman et al., 2022 ; Matena and Raffel, 2022 ; Ilharco et al., 2022 ) . Task Arithmetic ( Ilharco et al., 2023 ) represents each fine-tuned specialist by its task vector, the difference between its weights and those of the shared base model. A merge adds a scaled combination of task vectors back to the base, in the simplest case their average multiplied by a merge coefficient ( Ilharco et al., 2023 ; Ortiz-Jimenez et al., 2023 ) . Open-weight large language models (LLMs) now arrive as families of specialists for mathematics, code and other domains, built on shared bases ( Yang et al., 2024a ; Grattafiori et al., 2024 ; Yang et al., 2024b ; Hui et al., 2024 ; Cao et al., 2026 ) . Merging such specialists has become common practice, including in the training of production models ( Team Cohere et al., 2025 ) , and is supported by dedicated toolkits, benchmarks and studies at scale ( Goddard et al., 2024 ; He et al., 2025 ; Yadav et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2026 ; Hitit et al., 2026 ) . When specialists are fine-tuned for different tasks, however, they change shared weights in different directions, and averaging cancels part of each change, an effect usually called interference ( Yadav et al., 2023 ; Gargiulo et al., 2025 ) . We call a merge destructive when it falls substantially below the base model from which its specialists were fine-tuned, and harmless when it stays near or above that base. The standard way to reduce interference is to discard part of each task vector before averaging ( Yadav et al., 2023 ; Yu et al., 2024 ; Deep et al., 2024 ) . Each such prune-then-merge operator sets its keep rate in advance, whatever the disagreement between the specialists. These operators, like methods that tune the merge on data ( Matena and Raffel, 2022 ; Yang et al., 2023 ; Chopra et al., 2025 ) or derive it from the task vectors alone ( Marczak et al., 2025 ; Cheng et al., 2025 ) , leave open whether a merge will be destructive until it has been built and evaluated. We start from the identity underlying the ambiguity decomposition of ensembles ( Krogh and Vedelsby, 1994 ) . At every weight coordinate, the mean-squared power that averaging removes from the task vectors equals their variance across specialists. This variance is our measure of interference, and we compute it from the weights in the same pass as the average. Interference splits into cancellation, where specialists write comparable values of opposite sign, and dispersion, the remainder. Dispersion includes one-sided drift, in which one specialist moves a weight that the others leave near zero, and such drift can hold knowledge unique to that specialist ( Wang et al., 2024 ; Lu et al., 2024 ) . Under a working noise model, we show that the disturbance a merge injects into the base grows in proportion to the merge coefficient and to the square root of the interference. We call this estimate of the disturbance, available before merging, the interference score. We introduce Prism , a merge operator whose denoising threshold is set by interference, as Figure 1 illustrates. The operator averages the task vectors first and then soft-thresholds the average in each layer at the universal threshold of wavelet shrinkage ( Donoho and Johnstone, 1994 ; Donoho, 1995 ) . The noise level comes from the layer’s interference, a floor keeps a small share of each matrix’s coordinates, and one threshold scale serves all settings without data or tuning. A gate on the share of interference that comes from cancellation returns the plain average when that share is small, leaving one-sided drift intact. Across twenty-two merge configurations from four model families, with up to eight specialists in one merge, each outcome is either destructive or harmless. Seven merges are destructive at the default coefficient, six of them between public specialists. A threshold on the interference score flags five of the seven and none of the fifteen harmless merges, whereas statistics of sign disagreement, the conflict that sign election resolves ( Yadav et al., 2023 ) , are anti-predictive. We then fixed the score and this threshold, predicted the outcomes of fourteen further merges before evaluation, and found twelve predictions correct. Specialists are often built by continuing to pretrain a base model on domain text ( Gururangan et al., 2020 ; Hui et al., 2024 ) , and a practitioner who plans to merge them needs to know when more training would make the merge destructive. We therefore built two such specialists from one base model, one on Japanese web text and the other on biomedical abstracts, and tracked the pair’s score as training proceeded. At a fixed learning rate, the score grew roughly as the square root of the number of training tokens. Continued training at a higher learning rate further improved each specialist on its own domain but pushed the pair past the threshold. Plain averaging then became destructive as predicted, while Prism stayed near the base. Prism keeps each destructive merge above the threshold within evaluation noise of the base, where plain averaging falls far below it. The merge we study most closely combines a math specialist with a code specialist, as recent merging work does ( Yu et al., 2024 ; Cheng et al., 2025 ; He et al., 2025 ) . On this merge, Prism leads Task Arithmetic, two prune-then-merge operators ( Yadav et al., 2023 ; Deep et al., 2024 ) and a method that tunes the merge on data ( Chopra et al., 2025 ) at a shared coefficient. When we sweep the merge coefficient, these baselines collapse at large values while Prism degrades gradually. A merge whose coefficients are tuned by entropy minimization on unlabeled text ( Yang et al., 2023 ) also falls far below the base at the shared coefficient. Shrinkage helps a destructive merge but can forgo the gain that plain averaging brings to a harmless one, and our recipe therefore averages plainly below the score threshold and applies Prism above it. The score needs only the weights and minutes of CPU time, and we hope it makes a pre-merge check routine whenever public checkpoints are combined.

sections.heading: 2 Related Work
sections.text: Task Arithmetic ( Ilharco et al., 2022 ; Ilharco et al., 2023 ) established linear task-vector combination, and subsequent work has refined merging along three lines ( Liu et al., 2026 ; Cheng et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2024 ; Gargiulo et al., 2025 ) . Prune-then-merge methods include TIES-Merging, which combines magnitude trimming with cross-model sign election ( Yadav et al., 2023 ) , DARE, which drops entries at random and rescales the survivors ( Yu et al., 2024 ) , and DELLA, which drops entries with a probability that decreases with their magnitude ( Deep et al., 2024 ) . Training-free approaches include model matching ( Xu et al., 2024 ) , hierarchical merging ( Fu et al., 2025 ) , and trust-region constraints ( Sun et al., 2025 ) . Fisher averaging ( Matena and Raffel, 2022 ) , AdaMerging ( Yang et al., 2023 ) , LEWIS ( Chopra et al., 2025 ) and RAIN-Merging ( Huang et al., 2026 ) use auxiliary data. NeuroMerging decomposes task representations into neuronal subspaces ( Fang et al., 2025 ) , and NeuronMerge groups neurons by function ( Gu et al., 2025 ) . EMR-Merging ( Huang et al., 2024 ) uses task-specific masks, which requires knowing the task at test time. Spectral and subspace methods use spectrum flattening ( Marczak et al., 2025 ) , task singular vectors ( Gargiulo et al., 2025 ) , or task-vector guidance for data-free interference reduction ( Cheng et al., 2025 ) . PACT preprocesses task vectors through subspace alignment and offers a randomized-SVD variant ( Shi et al., 2026 ) . Twin-Merging dynamically combines shared and exclusive knowledge according to the input ( Lu et al., 2024 ) . We screen for collapse risk, a step absent from the merge operators evaluated here. The Prism repair soft-thresholds the coordinates of the averaged task vector in linear time, rather than pruning each task vector or computing singular value decompositions. It sets the threshold from the weights alone, through an exact variance identity and a noise model.

sections.heading: 5.1 Setup
sections.text: As in MergeBench ( He et al., 2025 ) , we vary model family and specialist domain, and we also vary the number of merged specialists. We merge specialists from two 7–8B families, Qwen2.5 ( Yang et al., 2024a ) and Llama-3.1 ( Grattafiori et al., 2024 ) , adding Mistral-7B and DeepSeek-7B for the breadth study. The main setting pairs Qwen2.5 Math ( Yang et al., 2024b ) with Coder ( Hui et al., 2024 ) at K = 2 K\!=\!2 , extended to K = 3 K\!=\!3 (Math, Coder, Instruct). For the shared task-vector protocol, we norm-scale by s k = min j ⁡ ‖ τ j ‖ 2 / ‖ τ k ‖ 2 s_{k}=\min_{j}\|\tau_{j}\|_{2}/\|\tau_{k}\|_{2} before averaging. By default, we apply an additional global coefficient c = 1 / K c=1/K to that average under Appendix B ’s convention. Baselines are Task Arithmetic ( Ilharco et al., 2023 ) , TIES ( Yadav et al., 2023 ) , DELLA ( Deep et al., 2024 ) , DARE ( Yu et al., 2024 ) , LEWIS ( Chopra et al., 2025 ) with the activation-based variant and weight-sparsity fallback compared in Appendix D.7 , AdaMerging ( Yang et al., 2023 ) , Greedy Soup ( Wortsman et al., 2022 ) , Fisher-Weighted Averaging ( Matena and Raffel, 2022 ) and the 2025 data-free Iso-C ( Marczak et al., 2025 ) and WUDI-Merging ( Cheng et al., 2025 ) . Headline task-vector comparisons use the shared coefficient, with baseline settings and sweeps summarized in Appendix D.9 , while Prism stays at its data-free default κ = 1.0 \kappa\!=\!1.0 . SLERP ( Shoemake, 1985 ) and Model Stock ( Jang et al., 2024 ) use their published recipes without our coefficient or norm scaling. Our evaluation spans six benchmarks, GSM8K ( Cobbe et al., 2021 ) , ARC-Challenge ( Clark et al., 2018 ) , MMLU ( Hendrycks et al., 2021 ) , TruthfulQA ( Lin et al., 2022 ) , HellaSwag ( Zellers et al., 2019 ) and WinoGrande ( Sakaguchi et al., 2020 ) , under lm-evaluation-harness ( Gao et al., 2024 ) , plus WikiText-2 perplexity ( Merity et al., 2016 ) , with GSM8K under strict-match extraction. Every reported mean is the average of the six task scores shown, and differences are absolute percentage points (pp). Generation metrics on GSM8K, MATH-500 ( Lightman et al., 2023 ) , HumanEval ( Chen et al., 2021 ) and MBPP ( Austin et al., 2021 ) use greedy decoding with one sample for each problem. A six-task mean carries a propagated standard error of at most 0.8 0.8 pp, so we treat sub-pp gaps as ties under Appendix D.4 ’s uncertainty estimate.

sections.heading: 5.4 Is it just conservative shrinkage?
sections.text: We test whether generic shrinkage ( Yu et al., 2024 ) explains the preserved capability with a control matched to Prism ’s update norm. Table 3 reports each update’s norm relative to the plain average. The baseline operators and community defaults write updates with 46 46 to 285 % 285\% of that norm, while Prism writes 2.2 % 2.2\% . For the matched control, one scalar multiplies every coordinate of the plain average to reach the same norm. The norm-matched control avoids collapse at both evaluated coefficients and stays close to the unmerged base on the six-task mean, perplexity and all four coding metrics. Its norm, however, is taken from Prism , whose thresholds set that norm from each layer’s interference without data or tuning. Where the control spreads this norm across 85.1 % 85.1\% of the coordinates, Prism concentrates it on the 0.1 % 0.1\% retained by thresholding. Prism ’s coding scores are higher than both the control’s and the base’s on all four EvalPlus metrics, reaching 65.9 65.9 on HumanEval against 62.2 62.2 and 62.8 62.8 .

sections.heading: 5.5 Data-dependent baselines need data to reach parity
sections.text: AdaMerging reaches 67.9 67.9 at its best point, a tie with Prism ’s 67.8 67.8 , after entropy minimization on unlabeled C4 text and a coefficient sweep. Greedy Soup adds neither specialist and returns the base model, and Fisher-weighted averaging falls to 47.5 47.5 in Appendix D.8 . Among data-free competitors, Iso-C reaches 66.6 66.6 when tuned away from its collapsing default, and WUDI-Merging diverges in every configuration of Appendix D.10 . SLERP at t = 0.5 t\!=\!0.5 ( Shoemake, 1985 ; Goddard et al., 2024 ) writes 1.27 × 1.27\times the norm-scaled average and collapses. Model Stock ( Jang et al., 2024 ) applies 2.4 × 2.4\times interpolation shrinkage toward the base and still loses 14.8 14.8 pp.

sections.heading: 5.6 Ablations and mechanism
sections.text: On Qwen K = 2 K\!=\!2 , soft thresholding beats hard truncation at the same threshold by 4.4 4.4 pp on the six-task mean in Table 3 . Truncation’s cost falls almost entirely on tasks that produce text, at 19.2 19.2 pp on GSM8K and up to 28.6 28.6 pp on HumanEval against 1.4 1.4 pp averaged over the five multiple-choice benchmarks in Figure 3 . Across threshold scales from κ = 0.25 \kappa\!=\!0.25 to 3 3 , the six-task mean varies by at most 0.5 0.5 pp, and the default scores highest in Table 6 . Replacing soft thresholding with magnitude pruning of the average at coherence-adapted layer rates lowers the mean by 3.7 3.7 pp at 7B and 6.9 6.9 pp at 1.5B, and Appendix D.5 shows that the gap closes at K = 3 K\!=\!3 , where interference is lower. Appendix C examines the layer-retention pattern. Where the calibrated threshold rather than the floor sets the keep rate ( κ = 0.5 \kappa\!=\!0.5 ), layer retention p l p_{l} tracks coherence data-free at r = 0.91 r\!=\!0.91 . Low coherence mixes sign conflict with task-exclusive drift, which the split of Eq. 3 separates, and the ρ \rho -gate returns the plain average when dispersion dominates. Appendix F shows that the coordinates removed by thresholding are predominantly conflict elements. In our low-rank simulation using SVD projections of full task vectors, Prism stays within 0.6 0.6 pp of its full-weight six-task mean across r ∈ { 8 , … , 128 } r\!\in\!\{8,\dots,128\} in Appendix D.12 .

sections.text: Table 4 and Figure 4 (a–d) cover twenty-two configurations across four families and K ∈ [ 2 , 8 ] K\!\in\![2,8] . sections.text: Interference, total power and signal power reach AUC 0.98 0.98 or higher, and interference also sets the repair’s variance scale. Mean incoherence 1 − CR ¯ 1-\overline{\mathrm{CR}} and ρ \rho are anti-predictive.

sections.heading: The gate.
sections.text: For raw Llama-3.1-8B K = 3 K\!=\!3 , gating ( ρ = 0.021 \rho\!=\!0.021 , λ = 0 \lambda\!=\!0 ) raises ungated Prism from 59.6 59.6 to Task Arithmetic’s 62.0 62.0 (base 60.2 60.2 ), as Table 19 shows. On Mistral-7B K = 2 K\!=\!2 at ρ = 0.093 \rho\!=\!0.093 , the gate likewise returns Task Arithmetic’s 59.9 59.9 , 2.5 2.5 pp above the base, in Table 4 .

sections.heading: A prospective test.
sections.text: With the statistic, convention and threshold fixed, twelve of the fourteen predictions made before evaluation were correct across three model families, including the harmless and destructive endpoints of the constructed pair. On the other two merges predicted to be destructive, R1-Distill + + Coder and Math-PRM + + Coder, naive averaging falls 18.4 18.4 and 14.4 14.4 pp below the base in Table 4 , whereas Prism keeps both within 0.5 0.5 pp of the base.

sections.heading: A controlled titration.
sections.text: We continued pretraining two Qwen2.5-1.5B specialists on disjoint Japanese web text and biomedical abstracts. At learning rate 10 − 4 10^{-4} , eight measured checkpoints follow an approximate square-root law through a harmless endpoint at one billion tokens for each specialist in Figure 4 . Extrapolated, the fitted law crosses the threshold near 7.5 7.5 billion tokens and reaches × 10 − 3 4.17\!\times\!10^{-3} , the lower edge of the destructive cluster in Table 4 , near 36 36 billion. Continuing at 5 × 5\times the rate reaches that cluster within a further billion tokens and improves own-domain perplexity (Japanese → 12.2 16.7\!\to\!12.2 , PubMed → 7.0 7.2\!\to\!7.0 ). As predicted before evaluation, the merge at this endpoint is destructive. Naive averaging loses 20.3 20.3 pp against the base, while Prism stays within 0.3 0.3 pp of it.

sections.heading: The recipe.
sections.text: Reported Prism results above evaluate the denoising operator, including its ρ < τ g \rho<\tau_{g} bypass gate. Our recipe uses naive averaging below the fixed score threshold and Eq. 4 ’s gated shrinkage above. All fifteen harmless configurations in Table 4 scored below the threshold and therefore keep the plain average, which scores 62.6 62.6 against the base’s 59.3 59.3 on Llama-3.1-8B R1-Distill with Tulu-3. The twenty-eight public pairs without a code specialist that we screened across three families all scored below half the threshold, as Appendix J details.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: We have shown that the variance of task vectors across specialists both predicts which merges collapse and calibrates their repair. Across twenty-two merges from four model families, the interference score built on this variance exceeded its threshold only for destructive merges, and twelve of the fourteen predictions made before evaluation were correct. Prism , which soft-thresholds the average of the task vectors, kept above-threshold destructive merges near the base without data or tuning. Because the score grows with training, model developers can track it to keep their specialists mergeable.

sections.heading: Ethics Statement
sections.text: All authors have read and adhere to the ICLR Code of Ethics. This work merges publicly released checkpoints and specialists we trained from public base models, and it evaluates the merges on public benchmarks. It involves no human subjects and collects no personal data. The continued pretraining uses public Japanese web text from FineWeb-2 and PubMed abstracts, as described in Appendix J . Merging can combine the weaknesses of its constituents along with their capabilities: pruning parameter updates could remove fragile safety alignment or amplify biases that conflict across specialists. Our screen and evaluations target capability benchmarks and do not measure safety behavior, so merged models need separate safety and alignment evaluation before deployment ( Lee et al., 2022 ) .

sections.heading: D.3 Interference Distribution
sections.text: We examine the distribution on which the threshold of Eq. 4 acts. The layer statistic σ l 2 = I ¯ l \sigma_{l}^{2}=\overline{I}_{l} averages interference across n l ∼ 10 8 n_{l}\!\sim\!10^{8} coordinates in the Qwen2.5-7B Math + + Coder merge. Across its 28 MLP layers, the sampled standardized aggregate has excess kurtosis 0.44 0.44 and skewness near zero, with mild heavy-tail deviations beyond | z | > 3 |z|\!>\!3 on a Q-Q plot. Layer coherence correlates negatively with mean interference ( r = − 0.41 r\!=\!-0.41 ). Under the common-component, independent-disturbance model, the empirical variance with divisor K K has expectation ( K − 1 ) / K (K{-}1)/K times the disturbance variance, including for K ∈ { 2 , 3 } K\!\in\!\{2,3\} . A constant rescaling of σ l \sigma_{l} can be offset algebraically by κ \kappa before the floor is applied. Using σ l \sigma_{l} rather than σ l / K \sigma_{l}/\sqrt{K} changes the threshold by K \sqrt{K} , at most about 2.8 2.8 over the studied range through K = 8 K=8 . The κ \kappa sweep in Table 6 spans a factor of 12 12 , wider than any of these convention changes, and the six-task mean stays between 67.3 67.3 and 67.8 67.8 across it. At K = 2 K\!=\!2 , an element-level σ ⁡ ( i ) \sigma(i) rests on a single squared difference. Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2610.03199v1 [cs.LG] 02 Oct 2026 Predicting and Repairing Merge Collapse in Large Language Models Jungseob Lee 1 omanma1928@korea.ac.kr Seungyoon Lee 1 dltmddbs100@korea.ac.kr Sugyeong Eo 2 s.eo@yonsei.ac.kr Hyeonseok Moon 3 hyns.moon@sookmyung.ac.kr Jaehyung Seo 4,† seojae777@konkuk.ac.kr Heuiseok Lim 1,† limhseok@korea.ac.kr 1 Korea University 2 Yonsei University Mirae Campus 3 Sookmyung Women’s University 4 Konkuk University Abstract Large language models fine-tuned from a shared base can be merged by averaging their task vectors, but some merges collapse far below the base model, and common merge operators give no warning before evaluation. We show that one statistic of the specialists’ task vectors both predicts this collapse and calibrates its repair. The power that averaging removes equals the variance of the task vectors across specialists, our measure of interference. Under a working noise model, the disturbance that a merge injects grows with the merge coefficient and with interference, yielding a pre-merge score. In our experiments on twenty-two merge configurations from four model families, only destructive merges exceed a threshold on this score. We find that statistics of sign conflict between specialists, a common target of existing merge operators, are anti-predictive. We then predicted the outcomes of fourteen merges before evaluating them, and twelve predictions were correct, including the destructive outcome of a specialist pair pushed past the threshold by continued pretraining. To address this collapse, we introduce Prism , an operator that averages the task vectors first and then soft-thresholds each layer at a level set by the layer’s interference. Without data or tuning, Prism keeps all five destructive merges above the threshold within evaluation noise of the base model, where plain averaging falls at least 14.4 points below it or collapses entirely. We apply Prism only above the threshold and keep the plain average for merges below it, which include all fifteen harmless ones. Code is available at https://github.com/js-lee-AI/PRISM . † † footnotetext: Corresponding authors. 1 Introduction Model merging combines several models fine-tuned from the same pretrained checkpoint into one model by operating directly on their weights, with no further training ( Wortsman et al., 2022 ; Matena and Raffel, 2022 ; Ilharco et al., 2022 ) . Task Arithmetic ( Ilharco et al., 2023 ) represents each fine-tuned specialist by its task vector, the difference between its weights and those of the shared base model. A merge adds a scaled combination of task vectors back to the base, in the simplest case their average multiplied by a merge coefficient ( Ilharco et al., 2023 ; Ortiz-Jimenez et al., 2023 ) . Open-weight large language models (LLMs) now arrive as families of specialists for mathematics, code and other domains, built on shared bases ( Yang et al., 2024a ; Grattafiori et al., 2024 ; Yang et al., 2024b ; Hui et al., 2024 ; Cao et al., 2026 ) . Merging such specialists has become common practice, including in the training of production models ( Team Cohere et al., 2025 ) , and is supported by dedicated toolkits, benchmarks and studies at scale ( Goddard et al., 2024 ; He et al., 2025 ; Yadav et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2026 ; Hitit et al., 2026 ) . When specialists are fine-tuned for different tasks, however, they change shared weights in different directions, and averaging cancels part of each change, an effect usually called interference ( Yadav et al., 2023 ; Gargiulo et al., 2025 ) . We call a merge destructive when it falls substantially below the base model from which its specialists were fine-tuned, and harmless when it stays near or above that base. The standard way to reduce interference is to discard part of each task vector before averaging ( Yadav et al., 2023 ; Yu et al., 2024 ; Deep et al., 2024 ) . Each such prune-then-merge operator sets its keep rate in advance, whatever the disagreement between the specialists. These operators, like methods that tune the merge on data ( Matena and Raffel, 2022 ; Yang et al., 2023 ; Chopra et al., 2025 ) or derive it from the task vectors alone ( Marczak et al., 2025 ; Cheng et al., 2025 ) , leave open whether a merge will be destructive until it has been built and evaluated. We start from the identity underlying the ambiguity decomposition of ensembles ( Krogh and Vedelsby, 1994 ) . At every weight coordinate, the mean-squared power that averaging removes from the task vectors equals their variance across specialists. This variance is our measure of interference, and we compute it from the weights in the same pass as the average. Interference splits into cancellation, where specialists write comparable values of opposite sign, and dispersion, the remainder. Dispersion includes one-sided drift, in which one specialist moves a weight that the others leave near zero, and such drift can hold knowledge unique to that specialist ( Wang et al., 2024 ; Lu et al., 2024 ) . Under a working noise model, we show that the disturbance a merge injects into the base grows in proportion to the merge coefficient and to the square root of the interference. We call this estimate of the disturbance, available before merging, the interference score. We introduce Prism , a merge operator whose denoising threshold is set by interference, as Figure 1 illustrates. The operator averages the task vectors first and then soft-thresholds the average in each layer at the universal threshold of wavelet shrinkage ( Donoho and Johnstone, 1994 ; Donoho, 1995 ) . The noise level comes from the layer’s interference, a floor keeps a small share of each matrix’s coordinates, and one threshold scale serves all settings without data or tuning. A gate on the share of interference that comes from cancellation returns the plain average when that share is small, leaving one-sided drift intact. Across twenty-two merge configurations from four model families, with up to eight specialists in one merge, each outcome is either destructive or harmless. Seven merges are destructive at the default coefficient, six of them between public specialists. A threshold on the interference score flags five of the seven and none of the fifteen harmless merges, whereas statistics of sign disagreement, the conflict that sign election resolves ( Yadav et al., 2023 ) , are anti-predictive. We then fixed the score and this threshold, predicted the outcomes of fourteen further merges before evaluation, and found twelve predictions correct. Specialists are often built by continuing to pretrain a base model on domain text ( Gururangan et al., 2020 ; Hui et al., 2024 ) , and a practitioner who plans to merge them needs to know when more training would make the merge destructive. We therefore built two such specialists from one base model, one on Japanese web text and the other on biomedical abstracts, and tracked the pair’s score as training proceeded. At a fixed learning rate, the score grew roughly as the square root of the number of training tokens. Continued training at a higher learning rate further improved each specialist on its own domain but pushed the pair past the threshold. Plain averaging then became destructive as predicted, while Prism stayed near the base. Prism keeps each destructive merge above the threshold within evaluation noise of the base, where plain averaging falls far below it. The merge we study most closely combines a math specialist with a code specialist, as recent merging work does ( Yu et al., 2024 ; Cheng et al., 2025 ; He et al., 2025 ) . On this merge, Prism leads Task Arithmetic, two prune-then-merge operators ( Yadav et al., 2023 ; Deep et al., 2024 ) and a method that tunes the merge on data ( Chopra et al., 2025 ) at a shared coefficient. When we sweep the merge coefficient, these baselines collapse at large values while Prism degrades gradually. A merge whose coefficients are tuned by entropy minimization on unlabeled text ( Yang et al., 2023 ) also falls far below the base at the shared coefficient. Shrinkage helps a destructive merge but can forgo the gain that plain averaging brings to a harmless one, and our recipe therefore averages plainly below the score threshold and applies Prism above it. The score needs only the weights and minutes of CPU time, and we hope it makes a pre-merge check routine whenever public checkpoints are combined. 2 Related Work Task Arithmetic ( Ilharco et al., 2022 ; Ilharco et al., 2023 ) established linear task-vector combination, and subsequent work has refined merging along three lines ( Liu et al., 2026 ; Cheng et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2024 ; Gargiulo et al., 2025 ) . Prune-then-merge methods include TIES-Merging, which combines magnitude trimming with cross-model sign election ( Yadav et al., 2023 ) , DARE, which drops entries at random and rescales the survivors ( Yu et al., 2024 ) , and DELLA, which drops entries with a probability that decreases with their magnitude ( Deep et al., 2024 ) . Training-free approaches include model matching ( Xu et al., 2024 ) , hierarchical merging ( Fu et al., 2025 ) , and trust-region constraints ( Sun et al., 2025 ) . Fisher averaging ( Matena and Raffel, 2022 ) , AdaMerging ( Yang et al., 2023 ) , LEWIS ( Chopra et al., 2025 ) and RAIN-Merging ( Huang et al., 2026 ) use auxiliary data. NeuroMerging decomposes task representations into neuronal subspaces ( Fang et al., 2025 ) , and NeuronMerge groups neurons by function ( Gu et al., 2025 ) . EMR-Merging ( Huang et al., 2024 ) uses task-specific masks, which requires knowing the task at test time. Spectral and subspace methods use spectrum flattening ( Marczak et al., 2025 ) , task singular vectors ( Gargiulo et al., 2025 ) , or task-vector guidance for data-free interference reduction ( Cheng et al., 2025 ) . PACT preprocesses task vectors through subspace alignment and offers a randomized-SVD variant ( Shi et al., 2026 ) . Twin-Merging dynamically combines shared and exclusive knowledge according to the input ( Lu et al., 2024 ) . We screen for collapse risk, a step absent from the merge operators evaluated here. Across twenty-two merges from four model families, the interference score built on this variance exceeded its threshold only for destructive merges, and twelve of the fourteen predictions made before evaluation were correct. Prism , which soft-thresholds the average of the task vectors, kept above-threshold destructive merges near the base without data or tuning. Because the score grows with training, model developers can track it to keep their specialists mergeable. Ethics Statement All authors have read and adhere to the ICLR Code of Ethics.
